name: LM2675M-5.0_NOPB
title: LM2675: 1 A step-down (buck) switching regulator, 260 kHz, 3.3 V, 5 V, 12 V and adjustable versions
summary: A 1 A buck regulator with its DMOS power switch, 260 kHz oscillator and loop compensation on chip, running from 8 V to 40 V (6.5 V to 40 V at reduced load). It comes in fixed 3.3 V, 5 V and 12 V versions and an adjustable version set by two resistors from 1.21 V to 37 V, in 8-pin SOIC and PDIP and a 16-pin WSON with exposed pad. A TTL-level ON/OFF input drops it to a 50 µA standby; cycle-by-cycle current limit with frequency foldback and thermal shutdown protect it. LM2675M-5.0/NOPB is the 5 V version in SOIC-8 in tubes of 95.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: A 5 V, 1 A step-down converter on the 5 V part, running from 8 V to 40 V. The internal FET switches VIN onto VSW; L1 and COUT filter the switched node to 5 V, and the Schottky D1 carries the inductor current while the FET is off. CB, from CB to VSW, powers the high-side gate drive. FB senses the output directly. ON/OFF is left open, which keeps the regulator on.

circuits.title: Fixed output voltage application (Figure 7-1)
circuits.description: The fixed-output circuit in which the 3.3 V, 5 V and 12 V characteristics are measured. An unregulated DC input feeds VIN, bypassed by CIN. The switch node drives L into the output capacitor and load, with D1 catching the inductor current to ground; CB bootstraps the gate drive. FB takes the regulated output, its wire routed clear of the inductor's field. ON/OFF is left open. The input loop (CIN, GND, D1) and the output ground return are the high-current paths, kept short over a ground plane.
notes: The design example for this circuit (5 V output, 12 V maximum input, 1 A) arrives at a 33 μH inductor (code L23), a 68 μF 10 V Sprague 594D or 100 μF 10 V AVX TPS output capacitor, a 1 A 20 V Schottky diode, a 15 μF 25 V Sprague 594D or 330 μF 16 V electrolytic input capacitor, and a 0.01 μF 50 V ceramic CB.

circuits.title: Adjustable output voltage application (Figure 7-6)
circuits.description: The adjustable version in the same buck arrangement, with the output set by a divider. R2 runs from the regulated output to FB and R1 from FB to ground, so the loop holds FB at the 1.21 V reference and VOUT = 1.21 V × (1 + R2/R1). Both resistors sit next to the FB pin on short leads. The rest matches the fixed circuit: CIN on VIN, the switch node into L, COUT and the load, D1 to ground, CB for the gate drive, ON/OFF open.
notes: The design example (20 V output, 28 V maximum input, 1 A) uses R1 = 1 kΩ and R2 = 15.4 kΩ, a 68 μH inductor (code L30), a 33 μF 25 V surface-mount or 120 μF 35 V through-hole output capacitor (code C20), a 1 A 40 V Schottky diode, and a 15 μF 50 V Sprague 594D or 330 μF 35 V electrolytic input capacitor.

operation.text: A monolithic buck regulator with an internal DMOS power switch rated for 1 A, a fixed 260 kHz oscillator and internal frequency compensation. Fixed 3.3 V, 5 V and 12 V versions and an adjustable version (1.21 V to 37 V) exist. Output voltage is held within ±1.5 % over line and load, the oscillator within ±10 %. At efficiencies above 90 % the board copper is the only heat sink needed. A complete supply needs five external parts: input capacitor, output capacitor, inductor, catch diode and bootstrap capacitor.

ON/OFF below 1.4 V puts the device in shutdown, with a typical standby current of 20 µA; the electrical characteristics give 50 µA typical. Above 1.4 V it starts switching and the output rises to regulation. The input is TTL-compatible; the pin floats high, enabling the regulator.

The loop holds FB equal to the internal 1.21 V reference. Fixed versions take FB straight from the output; the adjustable version uses a divider from VOUT to ground with its tap at FB, with a recommended R2 of 10 kΩ to 100 kΩ. An open divider breaks the loop and the output is not regulated. FB shorted to ground while enabled drives the output close to VIN, which can damage the load. The FB trace runs away from noisy areas.

Reaching the current-limit threshold ends the on-pulse immediately in any operating condition. The limit circuit also cuts the duty cycle below 50 % for a moment, which prevents subharmonic oscillation and inductor saturation; after the current drops back under the threshold the duty cycle rises again to its regulating value over a short relaxation time. Designs with an output above about 6 V and a duty cycle above about 50 % at minimum input can show large current-limit hysteresis after a fault: a large output capacitor draws enough recharge current (its stored energy is ½CV²) to trip the limit again and again before the output settles, and the output voltage is disturbed until the load current falls far enough for the limit circuit to reset. Shorting the output and then releasing it reveals the problem; a well-chosen design comes back smoothly. COUT = 47 µF and L = 22 µH were found to work under these conditions, and even with them the load current is kept at or below ICLIM/2 to keep the hysteresis small: 24 V in, 18 V out and 1.5 A of load call for a switcher whose current limit is at least 3 A.

Under severe overcurrent or a hard short, where inductor current rises past the limit cycle by cycle, the switching frequency is reduced automatically to protect the IC; below 100 kHz is typical for a hard short. Thermal shutdown is also built in.

Fixed versions: the inductor selection guide for the output voltage (3.3 V, 5 V or 12 V) is read at the maximum input voltage and maximum load current, giving an inductance and an inductor code (LXX); the code's row in the inductor part-number table lists Schott, Renco, Pulse Engineering and Coilcraft parts, through-hole and surface mount. For 5 V out, 12 V in and 1 A this is 33 µH, code L23. The adjustable version uses the E × T constant on the vertical axis of its guide instead of input voltage. Open-core inductors are placed so their flux does not cross the feedback, IC ground or COUT wiring.

Picked from the output capacitor tables by output voltage and the chosen inductance (fixed versions), or by a capacitor code from the code selection guide (adjustable version). The listed parts are Sprague 594D and AVX TPS surface-mount tantalums and Sanyo OS-CON, Sanyo MV-GX, Nichicon PL and Panasonic HFQ through-hole electrolytics. Other types are usable if their characteristics, especially ESR at 100 kHz, closely match the listed parts.

A Schottky diode is used for its fast switching and low forward drop. A shorted output is its worst case. It sits close to the IC on short leads and traces. Choices by reverse voltage and current are in the Schottky selection table; for a sustained short at the adjustable example a part of at least 2.2 A is recommended.

A low-ESR aluminum or tantalum capacitor between VIN and ground, close to the IC, stops large transients at the input. Its RMS current rating is at least half the DC load current; several capacitors in parallel can share it. Tantalum parts need surge-current testing by their maker (AVX TPS and Sprague 593D/594D are tested); a small series inductor in the supply line also limits surge stress. Ceramic input bypassing can cause severe ringing at VIN. For through-hole designs 330 µF electrolytics (Panasonic HFQ, Nichicon PL, Sanyo MV-GX) suit the examples; surface-mount electrolytics such as Sanyo CV-C or CV-BS, Nichicon WF or UR and NIC Components NACZ are options.
CB, between CB and VSW, charges to the voltage that drives the switch gate fully on. Every application uses a 0.01 µF, 50 V ceramic capacitor.
VIN both delivers load power and biases the internal circuits. Performance is specified for 6.5 V to 40 V at VIN. VIN is always bypassed by an input capacitor placed close to VIN and GND.

Fast-switching currents through wiring inductance produce voltage transients, so the high-current paths (the input loop through CIN, the switch node, D1 and the ground returns) are wide, short traces, with the external parts close to the IC over a ground plane or a single-point ground. On the adjustable version both feedback resistors sit near the IC and their wiring stays away from the inductor.
The 16-pin WSON allows more power dissipation than the SOIC and PDIP. Its die attach pad is connected to the PCB ground plane or a ground island. AN-1187 covers its CAD and assembly.

Fixed output example parts: CIN 15 µF 50 V solid tantalum (Sprague 594D), COUT 68 µF 16 V solid tantalum (Sprague 594D), D1 1 A 40 V surface-mount Schottky, L1 33 µH (L23, Coilcraft DO3316), CB 0.01 µF 50 V ceramic. Adjustable output example parts: CIN 15 µF 50 V and COUT 33 µF 25 V solid tantalum (Sprague 594D), D1 1 A 40 V surface-mount Schottky, L1 68 µH (L30, Coilcraft DO3316), CB 0.01 µF 50 V ceramic, R1 1 kΩ 1 %, R2 from the divider equation.
